source.title: Revisiting Weighted Aggregation in Federated Learning with Neural Networks
source.authors: Ze-Xi Li; Tao Lin; Xin-Yi Shang; Chao Wu

record.file_problem: Text is substantially readable, though some figures and symbols are garbled in extraction. The article and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own federated-learning generalization results and measures loss-landscape flatness, but does not test any listed version’s specific intervention or measure. Its results are related evidence about generalization and a measured property, so they are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.gate_note: The study reports top-1 test accuracy for global weight shrinking and learned aggregation methods, plus Hessian-based flatness measures. These results do not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, convolution versus fully connected training, optimizer comparisons, batch size, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Prior-work statements are not counted as results.
record.test_reason: Table 3 provides an unrecorded test of V3 in a new setting: FashionMNIST classifiers trained from scratch with federated local momentum SGD. LeNet outperforms the MLP under FedAvg and FedProx in both heterogeneity settings, but the comparison reverses under FedDyn at α=0.1. The extracted weight-shrinking rows themselves test none of V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that global weight shrinking can improve generalization with an appropriate factor balancing optimization and regularization, and that client coherence illuminates training dynamics and motivates FedLAW. Their proposed mechanisms include flatter loss landscapes and positive gradient coherence; these are their interpretations, not a test of V7's specific measure.
record.recipe_differences: Federated local training and server aggregation with learned or fixed aggregation weights; this is not the centralized training setup or intervention in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effect varies with aggregation-weight norm, client heterogeneity (IID versus NonIID), and architecture. The authors also describe dependence on local epochs and training stage.

fits_no_version.finding: In Table 1, suitable subunit aggregation-weight norms improve CIFAR-10 test accuracy over γ=1 for all three architectures in both client-distribution settings; the best norm varies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Global weight shrinking can improve federated image-classifier accuracy, depending on architecture, heterogeneity, and shrinkage strength.

fits_no_version.finding: Figures 4 and 10 associate adaptive global weight shrinking with improved test performance and flatter Hessian-based curvature than FedAvg.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive global weight shrinking can produce federated models with better test accuracy and lower Hessian-based sharpness.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 202, 2023
record.problems: The extracted results do not report training accuracy or train-test gaps. Table 1 provides test-accuracy values without uncertainty statistics; the paper says elsewhere that experiments were run three times and averaged. The study concerns federated aggregation, limiting its relevance to the listed centralized-training versions.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported conditions and outcomes are not extracted here, including the adaptive global weight shrinking results in Table 2, test-accuracy comparisons in Tables 3–8, further fixed-γ results in Table 9, and figure-only curves and flatness measures in Figures 1–10 and 15–17. They concern the same federated aggregation method but are outside the selected Table 1 fixed-γ comparison rows.

untested.parts: Fitting fixed random labels and comparing natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Increasing width beyond the zero-training-error threshold under training to convergence. Table 5 does not establish that threshold or report training error.
Whether local connectivity explains the architecture advantage; learning sparse local connections; initialization from a trained convolutional network.
Controlled adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparisons and their dependence on tuning. Client SGD and server Adam perform different operations here.
Batch-size comparisons under matched epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance. Client participation and local epochs are different interventions.
Dropout interventions, small-data underfitting, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.

Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, train-test gaps at similarly low training loss, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. Hessian curvature and test accuracy do not establish these.
Identifying memorized examples, removing them, and comparing retraining against matched random removal.

missing.what: Add paired FashionMNIST LeNet and MLP accuracy rows for the V3 comparisons under FedAvg, FedProx, and FedDyn, including the FedDyn reversal at α=0.1. Although rows_left_out declares Table 3 omitted, these comparisons are needed to represent the version actually tested.

record.verdict_notes: All 36 Table 1 values, baselines, architectures, and heterogeneity conditions match the supplied text. Appendix D states that results average three seeds and, within each run, test accuracy over the final 10 of 200 rounds; uncertainty intervals are not supplied. Training uses no data augmentation and generally includes local weight decay. Federated training alone does not exclude relevance to the versions: Table 3 supplies a direct convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison on FashionMNIST.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Generalization as width increases beyond zero training error; interpolation-threshold behavior.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization under tuning.
Large versus small batch effects and recipe adaptation.
Dropout effects and its interaction with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness and its ranking of train-test gaps. The paper reports Hessian-based flatness comparisons, but not the version’s measure or train-test gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
